title: Mapping-space descent along spines and increasing unions
statement: Use the local-smallness and universe conventions of [def-coef-presentable-infinity-category], and small simplicial sets, quasicategories, coherent functor categories, mapping spaces and limits of spaces from [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. For $n\geq0$, let $\operatorname{Sp}[n]\subseteq\Delta^n$ be the union of the vertices and the consecutive edges $\{i,i+1\}$, with their degeneracies. For every quasicategory $\mathcal C$, restriction $\operatorname{Fun}(\Delta^n,\mathcal C)\to\operatorname{Fun}(\operatorname{Sp}[n],\mathcal C)$ is an equivalence of quasicategories and induces equivalences on all mapping spaces. Let $L_0\subseteq L_1\subseteq\cdots$ be an increasing sequence of small simplicial sets, with degreewise union $L$, and let $F,G:L\to\mathcal C$ be diagrams. Restriction induces a natural equivalence of spaces $$\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{Fun}(L,\mathcal C)}(F,G)\simeq\lim_{n\in\mathbb N^{\mathrm{op}}}\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{Fun}(L_n,\mathcal C)}(F|_{L_n},G|_{L_n}).$$ This is a homotopy coherent limit, not merely an inverse limit of components, and the equivalence is natural in both diagrams. More generally, if $\mathcal C$ is locally small and $L$ is small, then $\operatorname{Fun}(L,\mathcal C)$ is locally small.

source.place: Proposition 5.3.4.13, proof (2)-(3) (spines) and (6) with the mapping-space argument behind Lemma 5.3.4.12 (inverse towers); local smallness follows from the same cellular restriction argument with small spaces. Read online; not archived in literature/. No Stacks tag states this coherent mapping-space calculus.

proof.text: First show that $i_n:\operatorname{Sp}[n]\hookrightarrow\Delta^n$ has the left lifting property against every inner fibration, using the lifting-class meaning of inner anodyne in [lem-coef-inner-anodyne-pushout-product]. For $n=0,1$ it is the identity. Inductively fill the face $\Delta^{\{0,\ldots,n-1\}}$ from its spine, leaving the last edge fixed. Starting from this face together with $\{n-1,n\}$, adjoin the faces on $S\cup\{n-1,n\}$ for nonempty $S\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n-2\}$ in increasing order of $|S|$. Each is attached along the inner horn missing the face $S\cup\{n\}$, opposite vertex $n-1$, whose position is $|S|$. The face omitting $n$ was in the initial face, and each face omitting an element of S was attached for a smaller S. The missing face itself is not present yet: it has the same S and cannot lie in any previously attached face. Thus this is precisely a horn attachment, of dimension $|S|+1\geq2$ and inner index $|S|$. Every nondegenerate simplex involving n is either the last vertex/edge or belongs to exactly one such pair of new faces. Successive inner-horn lifts solve every lifting problem for $i_n$; gluing agrees on the displayed intersections. This proves the claim with its base and inductive step, rather than assuming a spine theorem.

source.place: Example 1.5.7.7(a); explicit finite horn filtration supplied here for the path-graph case.

proof.text: Write $P=\operatorname{Fun}(\Delta^n,\mathcal C)$ and $Q=\operatorname{Fun}(\operatorname{Sp}[n],\mathcal C)$; these are quasicategories by [lem-cbc-internal-hom-quasicategory]. A boundary lifting problem for restriction $r:P\to Q$ transposes, by the internal-functor definition [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], to extending a map to $\mathcal C$ from $(\operatorname{Sp}[n]\times\Delta^m)\cup(\Delta^n\times\partial\Delta^m)$. The inclusion into $\Delta^n\times\Delta^m$ is the pushout product of $i_n$ with the boundary inclusion, so is inner anodyne by [lem-coef-inner-anodyne-pushout-product]. Since $\mathcal C\to\Delta^0$ is an inner fibration, the lift exists, including $m=0$. Hence r is a trivial Kan fibration. By [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper] it lifts every monomorphism. Lift $\varnothing\hookrightarrow Q$ to obtain a section s. Let J be the nerve of the groupoid with two objects and exactly one arrow between each ordered pair. Lift the monomorphism $P\times\{0,1\}\hookrightarrow P\times J$ with endpoints $sr,1_P$ and base map r constant on J. The unique arrows of J and their inverse triangles give a coherent natural equivalence $sr\simeq1_P$, while $rs=1_Q$. This proves that r is a functor equivalence as defined in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. By [lem-cbc-enhanced-functor-cone-calculus] it induces equivalences on all mapping spaces.

source.place: Example 1.5.7.7(b); boundary-lifting transposition and the section/invertible-interval argument are written out.

proof.text: Put $D_n=\operatorname{Fun}(L_n,\mathcal C)$ and $D=\operatorname{Fun}(L,\mathcal C)$. They are quasicategories by [lem-cbc-internal-hom-quasicategory]. By [lem-coef-infinity-isofibration-exponentiation] every $D_{n+1}\to D_n$ is an isofibration, hence an inner fibration. Write $U_E(x,y)=\{x\}\times_{E,\operatorname{ev}_0}\operatorname{Fun}(\Delta^1,E)\times_{\operatorname{ev}_1,E}\{y\}$ as in that node. Its morphism-space clause says that $U_n=U_{D_n}(F|_{L_n},G|_{L_n})$ is Kan and $U_{n+1}\to U_n$ is a Kan fibration. No surjectivity on vertices is inferred or needed.

source.place: Proposition 4.4.5.1 and Corollary 4.4.5.3; morphism-space lifting is Proposition 4.6.1.22 (01P8).

proof.text: In simplicial degree m, a map $L\times\Delta^m\to\mathcal C$ is exactly a compatible family of maps $L_n\times\Delta^m\to\mathcal C$: the products form the same degreewise union, and two restrictions agree wherever their domains meet. Conversely glue their values on each simplex, choosing any stage containing it; compatibility makes that value independent of the stage and preserves every simplicial operator. Thus $D=\varprojlim_nD_n$ strictly. Apply the identical gluing to maps $L\times\Delta^m\times\Delta^1\to\mathcal C$ with endpoint maps constant in the parameter at F,G. The endpoint conditions hold if and only if they hold at every stage. Therefore $U_D(F,G)=\varprojlim_n U_n$ as simplicial sets, with their projection cones. This uses only the internal-functor and degreewise-pullback formulas of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones].

source.place: Proposition 5.3.4.13(6), the strict inverse-limit identity expanded degree by degree.

proof.text: Apply [lem-coef-kan-fibration-tower-limit] to the tower $U_n$ of Step 3. Step 4 identifies its strict limit with $U_D(F,G)$, so the restriction cone exhibits $U_D(F,G)\simeq\lim_nU_n$ in spaces. The natural right-pinch maps of [lem-coef-infinity-pinch-comparison] identify $\operatorname{Map}_{D}(F,G)$ with $U_D(F,G)$ and identify every $\operatorname{Map}_{D_n}(F|_{L_n},G|_{L_n})$ with $U_n$. Their naturality under restriction identifies the two tower diagrams. Limits carry equivalences of diagrams to equivalences: by [lem-cbc-enhanced-functor-cone-calculus] a transformation of coherent diagrams $N(\mathbb N^{\mathrm{op}})\to\mathcal S$ whose vertex components are equivalences is an equivalence, and a cone is limiting exactly when its induced maps $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal S}(x,\text{apex})\to\operatorname{Map}(\Delta x,\text{diagram})$ are equivalences for every $x$; postcomposing with the diagram equivalence and precomposing with the apex equivalence $j_{D}$ preserves this criterion, since a functor equivalence induces equivalences on all mapping spaces. Consequently the cone on the pinched mapping spaces is limiting, and its comparison is the asserted restriction equivalence. It is a limit of entire spaces, including higher homotopies, because the cited tower theorem is a coherent-limit statement.

source.place: Lemma 5.3.4.11 (S a point), and Proposition 5.3.4.13(6), with Kerodon Proposition 4.6.5.10 (01L5).

proof.text: The restriction comparisons are natural in both diagrams with their coherent precomposition and postcomposition operations. By [lem-cbc-simplicial-composition-spine], these operations, their identities and their higher associativity homotopies are given by simplex and consecutive-edge restriction, naturally in simplicial functors. Every $D\to D_n$ and $D_{n+1}\to D_n$ is such a functor. Their restrictions therefore commute with this entire composition calculus, not only with composition of components. The degreewise gluing in Step 4 commutes with all these face and degeneracy restrictions; the same gluing holds with any additional simplicial parameter T since $L\times T\times\Delta^m$ is the union of $L_n\times T\times\Delta^m$. The pinch inclusions commute with the functors by [lem-coef-infinity-pinch-comparison]. Thus the cone used in Step 5 is a coherent cone of bifunctors in the endpoint diagrams. Its pointwise limiting property identifies it naturally with the limit: limits of functors to spaces are computed pointwise by [lem-coef-infinity-yoneda-presheaf-limits], applied in a sufficiently large universe. The two endpoint categories need only fit in that universe; no smallness of their object sets in the original universe is asserted. Hence the displayed equivalence is natural in both diagrams, including noninvertible transformations, rather than merely a separately chosen equivalence at each pair.

source.place: Agent expansion of the natural restriction comparison in Proposition 5.3.4.13(6); Kerodon 01F1 and 01L5 provide the relative evaluation and natural pinch models.

proof.text: For local smallness fix two diagrams F,G on a small L and let J consist of the values $F(v),G(v)$ for vertices v of L. This is a small family. By [lem-coef-infinity-small-full-subcategory], the replete full subcategory $E\subseteq\mathcal C$ on that family has a small quasicategory model $E_0$ with an equivalence $e:E_0\to E$. Both diagrams factor through E, because every vertex of every simplex of their images belongs to E. Moreover $\operatorname{Fun}(L,E)$ is the full subcategory of $\operatorname{Fun}(L,\mathcal C)$ on E-valued diagrams: an m-simplex has image vertices among the vertices of those diagrams. Its pinched mapping space from F to G is therefore exactly the one in $\operatorname{Fun}(L,\mathcal C)$. Postcompose with e and a quasi-inverse; the coherent inverse equivalences postcompose as well, and their components are equivalences by [lem-cbc-enhanced-functor-cone-calculus]. Hence $\operatorname{Fun}(L,E_0)\to\operatorname{Fun}(L,E)$ is a functor equivalence and induces mapping-space equivalences. The former functor simplicial set is small: in each degree its simplices are a subset of the set of all functions from the small graded set $L\times\Delta^m$ to the small graded set $E_0$, subject to the operator equations. Its mapping simplicial sets are small by the same counting argument and Kan by [lem-cbc-enhanced-functor-cone-calculus]. Thus the mapping space from F to G has a small Kan model, which is precisely local smallness [def-coef-presentable-infinity-category]. For empty L the functor category is the one-point quasicategory and the conclusion holds directly.
